notes.text: A king — Their desires exceed their reasons, which extended no farther than to the removal of Samuel's sons from their places, and the procuring some other just: and prudent assistance to Samuel's age. Nor was the grant of their desire a remedy for their disease, but rather an aggravation of it. For the sons of their king were likely to be as corrupt as Samuel's sons and, if they were, would not be so easily removed. Like other nations - That is, as most of the nations about us have. But there was not the like reason; because God had separated them from all other nations, and cautioned them against the imitation of their examples, and had taken them into his own immediate care and government; which privilege other nations had not.

Displeased — Because God was hereby dishonoured by that distrust of him, and that ambition, and itch after changes, which were the manifest causes of this desire; and because of that great misery, which he foresaw the people would hereby bring upon themselves. Prayed - For the pardon of their sin, and direction and help from God in this great affair.

Hearken — God grants their desire in anger, and for their punishment. Rejected me - This injury and contumely, reflects chiefly upon me and my government. Should not reign - By my immediate government, which was the great honour, safety, and happiness of this people, if they had had hearts to prize it.
So do they — Thou farest no worse than myself. This he speaks for Samuel's comfort and vindication.
Ye protest — That, if it be possible, thou mayst yet prevent their sin and misery. The manner - That is, of the kings which they desire like the kings of other nations.
Will take — Injuriously and by violence.
The gods — Before kings and princes.
Temple — Where the ark was. He was not permitted to enter into it. Magnified - For thou hast glorified thy word or promise unto me more than any other of thy glorious perfections.
The kings — A prophecy of the calling of the Gentiles. Hear - The gospel preached among then.
The ways — His wonderful counsel and gracious providences.

Perfect — Will finish the great work of my deliverance. Forsake not - Or, do not give over, the work of my salvation, which is thus far advanced, not by any human help, but by thy power and providence. This psalm is, by many of the Jewish doctors, esteemed the most excellent in the whole book. The omniscience of God is here asserted, ver. 1-6. Proved by two arguments; That he is everywhere present, ver. 7-12. And that he made us, ver. 13-16. This may fill us with pleasing admiration of God, ver. 17, 18. With an holy hatred of sin, ver. 19-22. And with an holy satisfaction in our own integrity, ver. 23, 24. To the chief musician, A psalm of David.

glossa.text:
*A psalm to David himself.* ((CASS.)) The captive, who had wept, as though Jerusalem and the temple were rebuilt, and as a fellow-citizen with that part of Jerusalem which was not captive, that is, with the angels, rejoices and praises first the benefits given him. In the person therefore of the Church, which is in the things above in hope, awaiting to be there in reality, he says, *I will confess.*

*I will confess to thee, O Lord.* First, he commends the benefits given him: secondly, he tells how these are spread abroad unto all, there, *Let them confess to thee, O Lord,* etc. *In the sight.* ((AUG.)) In praising I set before myself the angels, to whom I look to be made equal in dignity hereafter, as I am now. But these in the praise of God set before themselves nothing else but himself. *In the sight* therefore *of the angels,* in that purity wherein the angels behold thee, that in thee alone they may rest, I *will sing to thee.*

*For thy mercy.* ((ID.)) *All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth:* There are no other ways by which he came to us, there are no others by which we may come to him: let us render these to God, mercy in succouring, truth in judging. *Above every holy name of thine.* ((CASS.)) Or above thy holy name, when thy worship became known to us.
*In the soul.* And because in the soul a carnal multiplication can take place, he adds, *strength,* as though: I seek nothing else in the soul but strength.

*Let them confess.* ((ID.)) The second part, where it is said *dici*; read *dicit*, "he tells" how these good things are to be spread abroad unto all. As it were, after my example: *Let them confess,* etc. *All the words of thy mouth.* ((AUG.)) Which have now been revealed everywhere, and sent unto all nations, etc., *as far as* and thus, the fleece being dried, *they heard all the words,* etc.

*Great is the glory.* ((ID.)) If they are humble, they love and sing this; for if they exalt themselves, let them fear what follows. *For the Lord is high. He looketh on the low things.* ((CASS.)) Here is not the human condition, where the humble man is despised and the proud man regarded; but the Lord regards the humble.

*The high he knoweth afar off.* ((AUG.)) The proud man does not this, etc., *as far as* mourning this sojourning, whence it is subjoined.

*If I shall walk in the midst of tribulation.* Otherwise he does not quicken, save *in the midst of tribulation,* whence, *Blessed are they that mourn, woe to them that laugh.*

*Upon the wrath.* ((ID.)) This very thing, that they are angry with me, is thy chastisement upon them, that is, thy punishment. For to be angry is to them a punishment, not *noc* only a fault. While therefore thou permittest this, thou stretchest forth the hand of vengeance upon them all.

*Thy right hand.* God has not a right hand or a left, but the right hand of God is called eternal happiness, the left, temporal happiness. Sometimes therefore he does not save his saints in the left hand, but he always saves them in the right.
*He will repay.* ((AUG.)) What I cannot do, etc., *as far as* in whom the princes of the world found no sin, wherefore they should kill him.

notes.text: Having the same spirit of faith — Which animated the saints of old; David, in particular, when he said, I believed, and therefore have I spoken - That is, I trusted in God, and therefore he hath put this song of praise in my mouth. We also speak - We preach the gospel, even in the midst of affliction and death, because we believe that God will raise us up from the dead, and will present us, ministers, with you, all his members, "faultless before his presence with exceeding joy." Psalm cxvi, 10.

For all things — Whether adverse or prosperous. Are for your sakes - For the profit of all that believe, as well as all that preach. That the overflowing grace - Which continues you alive both in soul and body. Might abound yet more through the thanksgiving of many - For thanksgiving invites more: abundant grace.
Therefore — Because of this grace, we faint not. The outward man - The body. The inward man - The soul.

Our light affliction — The beauty and sublimity of St. Paul's expressions here, as descriptive of heavenly glory, opposed to temporal afflictions, surpass all imagination, and cannot be preserved in any translation or paraphrase, which after all must sink infinitely below the astonishing original.
The things that are seen — Men, money, things of earth. The things that are not seen - God, grace, heaven.
Our earthly house — Which is only a tabernacle, or tent, not designed for a lasting habitation.

glossa.text: *With you.* Not you with us, as inferiors, but that you may be our equals, if you will. And I well affirm concerning you, that we do all these things for the instructing of you by our example. So all things look to you: that the grace of God abounding in us may abound in you, and through you in others, and through you many it may abound in thanksgiving, that both you and they may give thanks to God. Unto the glory of God, that is, to show God glorious.

*For we know that if our earthly house of this habitation be dissolved, that we have a building,* etc. That is, we shall have an immortal body, if the body be dissolved through tribulations, and therefore, since it shall be so dissolved, so that the condition and the cause is set down first. *Not made with hands, but eternal.* That is, not made by the embrace of men, namely, not brought forth by the work of human generation nor increased by human fomentations, but ineffably framed together by God. *Eternal.* Because in it there shall be abiding without end.

notes.text: To eat bread — That is, to take any subsistence.
His relations — His mother and his brethren, ver. 31. But it was some time before they could come near him.

The scribes and Pharisees, Matt. xii, 22; who had come down from Jerusalem — Purposely on the devil's errand. And not without success. For the common people now began to drink in the poison, from these learned, good, honourable men! He hath Beelzebub - at command, is in league with him: And by the prince of the devils casteth he out devils - How easily may a man of learning elude the strongest proof of a work of God! How readily can he account for every incident without ever taking God into the question. Matt. xii, 24; Luke xi, 15.
Matt. xii, 31; Luke xii, 10.

Because they said, He hath an unclean spirit — Is it not astonishing, that men who have ever read these words, should doubt, what is the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost? Can any words declare more plainly, that it is "the ascribing those miracles to the power of the devil which Christ wrought by the power of the Holy Ghost?"

Then come his brethren and his mother — Having at length made their way through the crowd, so as to come to the door. His brethren are here named first, as being first and most earnest in the design of taking him: for neither did these of his brethren believe on him. They sent to him, calling him - They sent one into the house, who called him aloud, by name. Matt. xii, 46; Luke viii, 19.

Looking round on them who sat about him — With the utmost sweetness; He said, Behold my mother and my brethren -- in this preference of his true disciples even to the Virgin Mary, considered merely as his mother after the flesh, he not only shows his high and tender affection for them, but seems designedly to guard against those excessive and idolatrous honours, which he foresaw would in after ages be paid to her.

glossa.text: ((HIER.)) The house in which they come together is the primitive Church. The crowds which hinder the eating of bread are sins and vices, because *he that eateth the body of the Lord unworthily, eateth and drinketh judgment to himself, not discerning the body of the Lord ((I Cor. XI))*. Whence the Lord is turned into fury when he says: *Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you shall not have life ((Joan. VI))*.

*And when they had heard,* etc. The crowd throngs him, his own despise him as one mad, in which the salvation of the Gentiles is marked, and the envy of the Jews is reproved, of whom: *He came unto his own, and his own received him not ((Joan. VI))*.


[0193A]

*And the Scribes. ((BEDA.))* If any through slowness of mind do not understand the word of God, there yet remains a hope of salvation; if perchance they should understand, none. But for those who are unwilling to understand and who pervert what they do understand, there is no hope. Whence, *Scribes,* that is, the wise, etc. *From Jerusalem.* Which signifies that he was to be persecuted by his own fellow-citizens even unto death. We read above that a crowd followed him from Galilee and Jerusalem, and from beyond Jordan and about Tyre and Sidon, which are cities of the Gentiles: and the Scribes from Jerusalem were blaspheming: because the crowd of the people of the Jews conducted him with palms and praises; the Gentiles longed for him; the Scribes and the elders of the people were treating of his murder. *He hath Beelzebub.* Man of flies, or one having flies: by which name they surnamed the prince of demons, on account of the filth of the blood of the sacrifices.

*How can Satan,* etc. ((BEDA.)) Let them choose which they will. If Satan cannot cast out Satan, they say nothing against the Lord. But if he can, let them withdraw from his kingdom, which, being divided, cannot stand.

*And then shall he plunder his house. ((ID.))* He plundered the house, because he distributed all the parts of the world possessed by the devil to the apostles and to their successors, as provinces parted out among them, that they might convert the peoples to the faith.

*But he that shall blaspheme. ((HIER.))* Because he does not deserve to do penance so as to be received, who, understanding Christ, was saying that he was the prince of demons, etc., *as far as: For he that shall do and teach, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven ((Matth. V))*.

((BEDA.)) Matthew says ((Matth. XII)): *He that shall blaspheme against the Holy Ghost or the word,* etc. Where he shows that certain things are revealed in the world to come. Which is to be understood of the least matters, as of an idle word, of excessive laughter; for which even this life has earned pardon.

*For ever.* This against Origen, who promises pardon to all sinners after the judgment, when countless ages have passed.

*He shall be guilty of an everlasting sin. ((BEDA.))* Not because [it is said] that he is not a spirit: or that he is, but is not God: or that he is God, but less than the Father and the Son: because this comes not of diabolical envy, but of human ignorance, etc.

*Brethren. ((HIER.))* Not sons of Mary ever Virgin, as Helvidius lies: nor of Joseph by another wife, as others prate, but kinsmen.

((BEDA.)) The mother and the brethren, the people of the Jews of whom Christ is according to the flesh, stand outside in the literal sense. The crowd within the house, the Gentiles in the spiritual mystery. The Jews wish to see Christ outside, because, not seeking the spiritual understanding, they rather compel or seek him to come out to teach carnal things.

*Who is my mother. ((ID.))* He does not refuse obedience to a mother, who says: *Honour father and mother ((Exod. XX))*: but he shows that he owes more to his Father's mysteries than to a mother's affections, and he showed by example the same thing which he says in word: *He that loveth father or mother more than me, is not worthy of me ((Matth. X))*. Nor does he contemn his brethren injuriously, but he sets the spiritual work before kinship, teaching that the bond of hearts is better than the bond of bodies.

*Behold my mother,* etc. ((HIER.)) That we may know that we are both his brethren and his mother, if we shall have done the will of his Father, so that we may be co-heirs, because he discerns not by sexes but by deeds. Sister and brother by believing, mother by preaching, while through preaching the love of Christ, as it were Christ himself, is begotten in the heart of the hearer.

notes.text: Where art thou? — This enquiry after Adam may be looked upon as a gracious pursuit in order to his recovery. If God had not called to him to reduce him, his condition had been as desperate as that of fallen angels.

I heard thy voice in the garden: and I was afraid — Adam was afraid because he was naked; not only unarmed, and therefore afraid to contend with God, but unclothed and therefore afraid so much as to appear before him.

Who told thee that thou wast naked? — That is, how camest thou to be sensible of thy nakedness as thy shame? Hast thou eaten of the tree? - Tho' God knows all our sins, yet he will know them from us, and requires from us an ingenuous confession of them, not that he may be informed, but that we may be humbled. Whereof I commanded thee not to eat of it, I thy maker, I thy master, I thy benefactor, I commanded thee to the contrary. Sin appears most plain and most sinful in the glass of the commandment.

What is this that thou hast done? — Wilt thou own thy fault? Neither of them does this fully. Adam lays all the blame upon his wife: She gave me of the tree - Nay, he not only lays the blame upon his wife, but tacitly on God himself. The woman thou gavest me, and gavest to be with me as my companion, she gave me of the tree. Eve lays all the blame upon the serpent; the serpent beguiled me. The prisoners being found guilty by their own confession, besides the infallible knowledge of the Judge, and nothing material being offered in arrest of judgment, God immediately proceeds to pass sentence, and in these verses he begins (where the sin began) with the serpent. God did not examine the serpent, nor ask him what he had done, but immediately sentenced him, (1.) Because he was already convicted of rebellion against God. (2.) Because he was to be forever excluded from pardon; and why should any thing be said to convince and humble him, who was to find no place for repentance?

To testify a displeasure against sin, God fastens a curse upon the serpent, Thou art cursed above all cattle — Even the creeping things, when God made them, were blessed of him, chap. i, 22, but sin turned the blessing into a curse. Upon thy belly shalt thou go - No longer upon feet, or half erect, but thou shalt crawl along, thy belly cleaving to the earth. Dust thou shalt eat - Which signifies a base and despicable condition.

And I will put enmity between thee and the woman — The inferior creatures being made for man, it was a curse upon any of them to be turned against man, and man against them. And this is part of the serpent's curse.

1. A perpetual reproach is fastened upon him. Under the cover of the serpent he is here sentenced to be, (1.) Degraded and accursed of God. It is supposed, pride was the sin that turned angels into devils, which is here justly punished by a great variety of mortifications couched under the mean circumstances of a serpent, crawling on his belly, and licking the dust. (2.) Detested and abhorred of all mankind: even those that are really seduced into his interest, yet profess a hatred of him. (3.) Destroyed and ruined at last by the great Redeemer, signified by the bruising of his head; his subtle politics shall be all baffled, his usurped power entirely crushed.

2. A perpetual quarrel is here commenced between the kingdom of God, and the kingdom of the devil among men; war proclaimed between the seed of the woman, and the seed of the serpent, Rev. xii, 7. It is the fruit of this enmity, (1.) That there is a continual conflict between God's people and him. Heaven and hell can never be reconciled, no more can Satan and a sanctified soul. (2.) That there is likewise a continual struggle between the wicked and the good. And all the malice of persecutors against the people of God is the fruit of this enmity, which will continue while there is a godly man on this side heaven, and a wicked man on this side hell.

3. A gracious promise is here made of Christ as the deliverer of fallen man from the power of Satan. By faith in this promise, our first parents, and the patriarchs before the flood, were justified and saved; and to this promise, and the benefit of it, instantly serving God day and night they hoped to come. Notice is here given them of three things concerning Christ. (1.) His incarnation, that he should be the seed of the woman. (2.) His sufferings and death, pointed at in Satan's bruising his heel, that is, his human nature. (3.) His victory over Satan thereby. Satan had now trampled upon the woman, and insulted over her; but the seed of the woman should be raised up in the fulness of time to avenge her quarrel, and to trample upon him, to spoil him, to lead him captive, and to triumph over him, Colossians ii, 15.

16. We have here the sentence past upon the woman; she is condemned to a state of sorrow and a state of subjection: proper punishments of a sin in which she had gratified her pleasure and her pride. (1.) She is here put into a state of sorrow; one particular of which only is instanced in, that in bringing forth children, but it includes all those impressions of grief and fear which the mind of that tender sex is most apt to receive, and all the common calamities which they are liable to. It is God that multiplies our sorrows, I will do it: God, as a righteous Judge, doth it, which ought to silence us under all our sorrows; as many as they are we have deserved them all, and more: nay, God as a tender Father doth it for our necessary correction, that we may be humbled for sin, and weaned from it. (2.) She is here put into a state of subjection: the whole sex, which by creation was equal with man, is for sin made inferior.

glossa.text:
« And when they had heard, » etc. ((AUG., l. II de Gen. ad litt., c. 33.)) For at that hour it was fitting that such as they should be visited, because they had fallen away from the light of truth, etc., *as far as* he may be believed to have appeared to the bodily senses by a local and temporal motion.

« He hid himself, » etc. ((AUG., ibid.)) When God turns away his face within and man is troubled, things like madness come about, through excessive fear and shame, with a hidden instinct also not resting: so that unknowing they did things which should signify something to those who came after, for whose sake these things are written.

« At the afternoon air. » Whence at the ninth hour Christ gave up the spirit ((Matth. XXVII)). He was crucified at the sixth hour, that man might be restored at the same hour at which he was cast out of paradise.

« In the midst of the tree of paradise. » He hides himself who, turned away from the precept of the Creator, lives by the will of his own error and choice.
« And the Lord God called Adam. » ((AUG., ubi supra, c. 34.)) By rebuking, that is, not by being ignorant, etc., *as far as* but now we are not reporting things signified, but defending things done.

« And he said: I heard thy voice, » etc. *((AUG., ubi supra, c. 34.)) Historically.* It is probable that a human form was wont to appear to the first men through a fitting creature, etc., *as far as* and there followed that of which they were ashamed.

« Thy voice, » etc. *((ISID., in Gen. tom. V.)) Mystically.* He answers that, having heard his voice, he had hidden himself, etc., *as far as* and not to obey the precept of God.

« And God called Adam, » etc. ((GREG.)) Because he saw him fallen into fault, now under sin, as though hidden from the eyes of truth, because he does not approve the darkness of his error, he is as it were ignorant where the sinner is, and calls him and seeks him, saying: « Adam, where art thou? » While he calls, he signifies that he is calling him back to penance; while he seeks him, he intimates that he knows not sinners justly condemned.

« And Adam said: The woman whom thou gavest, » etc. ((AUG.)) He does not say, I have sinned: for pride has the deformity of confusion, not the humility of confession. But it was written for this, and the questions were put for this, that they might be written truly and profitably, so that we may know with how great a disease of pride they labour who today try to refer evil to the Creator, and, if they do any good, to attribute it to themselves.

« The woman whom thou gavest, » etc. As though she had been given for this, that she herself should not obey the man, and both of them God.

« The woman whom thou gavest, » etc. ((GREG., lib. IV Mor., c. 27, tom. I, col. 661.)) In four ways is sin committed in the heart, etc., *as far as* at the last it is nourished by the seduction of false hope, or by the obstinacy of wretched despair .

« And the Lord God said to the woman, » etc. ((AUG.)) Neither does she confess the sin, but refers it to another — in an unequal sex, with equal haughtiness. Yet David, born of these, says unto the end of the world: « I said: Lord, be merciful to me, heal my soul, for I have sinned against thee ((Psal. XL)). » This ought to have been said by those two: but God does not yet regard the necks of sinners: there remained the labours and sorrows of death, and the wearing away of the world, and the grace of God, which comes to help in due time, teaching the afflicted not to presume of themselves.

« The serpent deceived, » etc. As though anyone's persuasion should prevail over God's precept.

« The serpent deceived me, » etc. ((AUG., ibid., lib. II, c. 30.)) How by these words, etc., *as far as* since with that food he did not see her to be dead.

((AUG., ibid., c. 28.)) It is to be noted that the devil was not permitted to tempt the woman, etc., *as far as* but reason shows that on this account he envied man.

((ALC.)) The sin of the angel was left unspoken, that of man laid open, because the one was incurable, the other was cured.

« She saw therefore, » etc. ((STRAB.)) She is plainly shown to be inexcusable, since it was open to her, under such deliberation, to mark the wiles of the enemy.

« And the Lord God said, » etc. ((AUG., ubi supra, c. 36.)) This whole sentence is figurative. Where nevertheless it must be believed that all things were said. The serpent is not asked why he did it, because it was not he that did it by his own will and nature, but the devil out of him, and through him, and in him: who already for his impiety and pride had been destined for eternal fire. To him, therefore, is referred what is said to the serpent, and it is shown what he will be to the human race.

*Mystically.* « And the Lord God said to the serpent, » etc. ((AUG., de Gen. cont. Manich., lib. II, c. 17.)) The serpent, unquestioned, is the first to receive punishment, etc., *as far as* that he may shut out the very beginning of the evil suggestion.

« Upon thy breast, » etc. ((HIERON.)) « Belly » the Seventy added, but in the Hebrew there is « breast In the Hebrew it is *gahon*, which signifies *belly* and *breast*. » only, that he might lay open the craft and cunning of his thoughts, that is, that his every step is of wickedness and of fraud.

 « With breast and belly thou shalt creep. » ((GREG., lib. XXI Mor., c. 2.)) The evil of lechery is committed either in thought or in deed. For when the enemy is driven out from the accomplishment of the deed, he labours to defile the secret places of thought. He creeps with the belly, when, slippery, through the human members made subject to him, he practises lechery in deed. He crawls with the breast, when he defiles in thought. But because it is through thought that one comes to deeds, he is described as creeping first with the breast and afterwards with the belly.

« I will put enmities between thee and the woman . . . She shall crush thy head, » etc. ((GREG. l. I Mor., c. 38.)) To crush the serpent's head is to root out the beginnings of his suggestion from the entrance of the heart by the hand of watchful consideration; for when he is caught at the very outset, he contrives to strike the heel, because the man whom he does not strike in the first temptation he aims to deceive at the end. But if the heart is corrupted in the temptation, the middle and the end of the action that follows are possessed by the enemy, because he sees the whole tree bearing fruit for him, the tree which he has vitiated at the root with the tooth of his venom.

((HIERON.)) « She shall keep thy heel, and thou shalt crush her heel. » It stands better in the Hebrew: « She shall crush thy head, and thou shalt crush her heel, » because both our steps are hampered by the serpent, and the Lord shall crush Satan under her feet.

notes.text: Mark — Observe them accurately and punish them as they deserve. Stand - At thy tribunal.

Forgiveness — Thou art able and ready to forgive repenting sinners. Feared - Not with a slavish, but with a childlike fear. This mercy of thine is the foundation of all religion, without which men would desperately proceed in their impious courses.
I wait — That he would pardon my sins.
They — Whether soldiers that keep the night-watches in an army, or the priests or Levites who did so in the temple.

Israel — Every true Israelite. Plenteous - Abundantly sufficient for all persons who accept it upon God's terms. David testifies his humility, and exhorts Israel to trust in God, ver. 1-3. A song of degrees of David.

glossa.text:
*A canticle of degrees.* ((ID.)) The eleventh degree, etc., *as far as* a glad conclusion is set down with the certainty of pardon, there, *Let Israel hope in the Lord.*

*Out of the depths.* ((AUG.)) He who feels himself in the deep, etc., *as far as* as the Scripture says: *The sinner, when he shall have come into the depth of vices, contemneth.*

*Who shall abide it.* ((ID.)) Because well nigh all human life is barked at round about by sins, and every conscience is accused by its own thoughts. That heart is not chaste which presumes upon its own justice. Let it therefore presume upon the mercy of God, *For with him there is propitiation,* whence he subjoins:

*For with thee there is propitiation.* As it were: In what hope dost thou cry? Because there is mercy in thee, wherefore he speaks thus: Or join it thus.

((AUG.)) No man can abide it, etc., *as far as* one hope therefore there is: *For with thee there is propitiation,* etc., *For thy law's sake,* ((ID.)) I have waited for the *law* of mercy, etc., *as far as* and thou hast given this law in the very necessity.

*The morning.* ((ID.)) Let him hope in the morning watch who hopes for nothing else from God than immortality. *From the morning watch,* etc., *as far as* thence in the law the head and the tail of the victim were offered to the Lord. *Let Israel hope in the Lord.* ((CASS.)) The second part, where is the glad conclusion: Secure concerning himself, he preaches that they should hope always in the Lord. As it were, as his soul has hoped, so let Israel hope.
*And he shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities.* ((ID.)) Here he has now said what that one shall do, whom he called merciful and plentiful.

notes.text: Having the same spirit of faith — Which animated the saints of old; David, in particular, when he said, I believed, and therefore have I spoken - That is, I trusted in God, and therefore he hath put this song of praise in my mouth. We also speak - We preach the gospel, even in the midst of affliction and death, because we believe that God will raise us up from the dead, and will present us, ministers, with you, all his members, "faultless before his presence with exceeding joy." Psalm cxvi, 10.

For all things — Whether adverse or prosperous. Are for your sakes - For the profit of all that believe, as well as all that preach. That the overflowing grace - Which continues you alive both in soul and body. Might abound yet more through the thanksgiving of many - For thanksgiving invites more: abundant grace.
Therefore — Because of this grace, we faint not. The outward man - The body. The inward man - The soul.

Our light affliction — The beauty and sublimity of St. Paul's expressions here, as descriptive of heavenly glory, opposed to temporal afflictions, surpass all imagination, and cannot be preserved in any translation or paraphrase, which after all must sink infinitely below the astonishing original.
The things that are seen — Men, money, things of earth. The things that are not seen - God, grace, heaven.
Our earthly house — Which is only a tabernacle, or tent, not designed for a lasting habitation.

glossa.text: *With you.* Not you with us, as inferiors, but that you may be our equals, if you will. And I well affirm concerning you, that we do all these things for the instructing of you by our example. So all things look to you: that the grace of God abounding in us may abound in you, and through you in others, and through you many it may abound in thanksgiving, that both you and they may give thanks to God. Unto the glory of God, that is, to show God glorious.

*For we know that if our earthly house of this habitation be dissolved, that we have a building,* etc. That is, we shall have an immortal body, if the body be dissolved through tribulations, and therefore, since it shall be so dissolved, so that the condition and the cause is set down first. *Not made with hands, but eternal.* That is, not made by the embrace of men, namely, not brought forth by the work of human generation nor increased by human fomentations, but ineffably framed together by God. *Eternal.* Because in it there shall be abiding without end.

notes.text: To eat bread — That is, to take any subsistence.
His relations — His mother and his brethren, ver. 31. But it was some time before they could come near him.

The scribes and Pharisees, Matt. xii, 22; who had come down from Jerusalem — Purposely on the devil's errand. And not without success. For the common people now began to drink in the poison, from these learned, good, honourable men! He hath Beelzebub - at command, is in league with him: And by the prince of the devils casteth he out devils - How easily may a man of learning elude the strongest proof of a work of God! How readily can he account for every incident without ever taking God into the question. Matt. xii, 24; Luke xi, 15.
Matt. xii, 31; Luke xii, 10.

Because they said, He hath an unclean spirit — Is it not astonishing, that men who have ever read these words, should doubt, what is the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost? Can any words declare more plainly, that it is "the ascribing those miracles to the power of the devil which Christ wrought by the power of the Holy Ghost?"

Then come his brethren and his mother — Having at length made their way through the crowd, so as to come to the door. His brethren are here named first, as being first and most earnest in the design of taking him: for neither did these of his brethren believe on him. They sent to him, calling him - They sent one into the house, who called him aloud, by name. Matt. xii, 46; Luke viii, 19.

Looking round on them who sat about him — With the utmost sweetness; He said, Behold my mother and my brethren -- in this preference of his true disciples even to the Virgin Mary, considered merely as his mother after the flesh, he not only shows his high and tender affection for them, but seems designedly to guard against those excessive and idolatrous honours, which he foresaw would in after ages be paid to her.

glossa.text: ((HIER.)) The house in which they come together is the primitive Church. The crowds which hinder the eating of bread are sins and vices, because *he that eateth the body of the Lord unworthily, eateth and drinketh judgment to himself, not discerning the body of the Lord ((I Cor. XI))*. Whence the Lord is turned into fury when he says: *Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you shall not have life ((Joan. VI))*.

*And when they had heard,* etc. The crowd throngs him, his own despise him as one mad, in which the salvation of the Gentiles is marked, and the envy of the Jews is reproved, of whom: *He came unto his own, and his own received him not ((Joan. VI))*.


[0193A]

*And the Scribes. ((BEDA.))* If any through slowness of mind do not understand the word of God, there yet remains a hope of salvation; if perchance they should understand, none. But for those who are unwilling to understand and who pervert what they do understand, there is no hope. Whence, *Scribes,* that is, the wise, etc. *From Jerusalem.* Which signifies that he was to be persecuted by his own fellow-citizens even unto death. We read above that a crowd followed him from Galilee and Jerusalem, and from beyond Jordan and about Tyre and Sidon, which are cities of the Gentiles: and the Scribes from Jerusalem were blaspheming: because the crowd of the people of the Jews conducted him with palms and praises; the Gentiles longed for him; the Scribes and the elders of the people were treating of his murder. *He hath Beelzebub.* Man of flies, or one having flies: by which name they surnamed the prince of demons, on account of the filth of the blood of the sacrifices.

*How can Satan,* etc. ((BEDA.)) Let them choose which they will. If Satan cannot cast out Satan, they say nothing against the Lord. But if he can, let them withdraw from his kingdom, which, being divided, cannot stand.

*And then shall he plunder his house. ((ID.))* He plundered the house, because he distributed all the parts of the world possessed by the devil to the apostles and to their successors, as provinces parted out among them, that they might convert the peoples to the faith.

*But he that shall blaspheme. ((HIER.))* Because he does not deserve to do penance so as to be received, who, understanding Christ, was saying that he was the prince of demons, etc., *as far as: For he that shall do and teach, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven ((Matth. V))*.

((BEDA.)) Matthew says ((Matth. XII)): *He that shall blaspheme against the Holy Ghost or the word,* etc. Where he shows that certain things are revealed in the world to come. Which is to be understood of the least matters, as of an idle word, of excessive laughter; for which even this life has earned pardon.

*For ever.* This against Origen, who promises pardon to all sinners after the judgment, when countless ages have passed.

*He shall be guilty of an everlasting sin. ((BEDA.))* Not because [it is said] that he is not a spirit: or that he is, but is not God: or that he is God, but less than the Father and the Son: because this comes not of diabolical envy, but of human ignorance, etc.

*Brethren. ((HIER.))* Not sons of Mary ever Virgin, as Helvidius lies: nor of Joseph by another wife, as others prate, but kinsmen.

((BEDA.)) The mother and the brethren, the people of the Jews of whom Christ is according to the flesh, stand outside in the literal sense. The crowd within the house, the Gentiles in the spiritual mystery. The Jews wish to see Christ outside, because, not seeking the spiritual understanding, they rather compel or seek him to come out to teach carnal things.

*Who is my mother. ((ID.))* He does not refuse obedience to a mother, who says: *Honour father and mother ((Exod. XX))*: but he shows that he owes more to his Father's mysteries than to a mother's affections, and he showed by example the same thing which he says in word: *He that loveth father or mother more than me, is not worthy of me ((Matth. X))*. Nor does he contemn his brethren injuriously, but he sets the spiritual work before kinship, teaching that the bond of hearts is better than the bond of bodies.

*Behold my mother,* etc. ((HIER.)) That we may know that we are both his brethren and his mother, if we shall have done the will of his Father, so that we may be co-heirs, because he discerns not by sexes but by deeds. Sister and brother by believing, mother by preaching, while through preaching the love of Christ, as it were Christ himself, is begotten in the heart of the hearer.

registers.label: Spare
lines: We give you thanks, O Lord, with our whole heart.
Though we walk in trouble, your hand keeps us alive.
The people once cried out for a king like the nations.
But you alone are our King; we will not be ruled by less.
Whoever does the will of God is sister, brother, mother to Christ.
Then we are kin; we belong to one another.
Come, let us worship the God who reaches down to us.
We come with our whole heart. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: When you call, God answers and stretches a hand into the middle of your trouble, and the strength of your soul comes back.
We give you thanks with our whole heart.
Israel begged for a king to fight their battles and forgot the God who carried them, yet still God would not let them go.
We give you thanks with our whole heart.
Jesus looks around the crowded room and says: here are my mother and my brothers, anyone who does the will of God.
We give you thanks with our whole heart.
So come in, all of you who were far off; you are family now, and there is a place for you in this house.
We give you thanks with our whole heart, and we will not be moved.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: You stretch out your hand; you keep us alive.
We thank you with our whole heart.
You alone are King; we trust no lesser throne.
We thank you with our whole heart.
All who do God's will are sister and brother here.
We thank you with our whole heart.
Come in, you are kin; come, let us worship.
We thank you with our whole heart. Amen.
